ad.intro1.html: SPF says which servers may send for the domain; DMARC tells recipients what to do with mail that does not authenticate. The panel writes them on Cloudflare with the account already linked to the domain, the same one it uses for DKIM rotation. If a record of that kind already exists, it leaves it alone: it stops and shows it to you.
ad.intro2.html: The check looks at the content of the records, not the name: a google-site-verification at the apex has nothing to do with SPF and must not stop it from being created. And if there were two records, it says so: two SPF records on the same name give permerror and SPF stops working altogether (RFC 7208 §4.5), two DMARC records are both discarded (RFC 9989). These failures give no signal: mail keeps leaving, and one day it starts landing in spam.
ad.intro3.html: “Set up everything” runs the whole chain for this domain, in one click: DKIM keys and record, SPF, the report mailbox, DMARC in monitoring mode, autoconfig, the two SRV records, and then MTA-STS in full: the include line in nginx, the port 443 setup, the jail, the mta-sts CNAME, the proxy turned off on that name, a certificate covering it, the wait for propagation, the policy test and finally the TXT record. DNS, nginx and certificate do not work separately if you want MTA-STS: it is one chain, run by one sequence, the same as the “Activate MTA-STS” button, which does it for every domain instead of one. At the first step that fails it stops and explains what is missing.
ad.noReportBoxWhy: Today mail addressed to {address} goes nowhere: there is no mailbox with that name, and no forwarding sends it elsewhere. Until that changes, publishing DMARC would help little: the reports would leave and all bounce.
ad.noRotation: SPF and DMARC contain no keys: they are public policy statements, changed when the server or the policy changes, not on a schedule. That is why there is no rotation here: it would be fake maintenance, and every automatic SPF change is a chance to stop outgoing mail.

Turn on MTA-STS on every domain?

The panel runs, in order: the include line in nginx, the 443 configuration, the fail2ban jail, one mta-sts CNAME per domain, the Cloudflare proxy off on those names, a certificate covering them, the policy test, and finally the TXT record.

The TXT record is published ONLY for the domains whose policy really answers. At the first step that fails it stops and explains.

No record other than mta-sts is touched: a wildcard *.domain, if any, stays exactly as it is.

Where it creates or fixes a record, the sequence waits for the DNS to propagate before testing the policy: so it can take a few minutes. The work goes on on the server even if you close the page.

cfi.intro1.html: Both panels sit behind Cloudflare, so every request comes from an edge address. The real address of whoever knocks is in the CF-Connecting-IP header, and the panel trusts it only if the connection comes from an address it recognizes as Cloudflare — otherwise anyone could write whatever they like in it and forge their entry in the logs.
cfi.intro2.html: That list is written by hand inside the panel and must stay the same as the official one. If Cloudflare adds a range and starts serving from it, the panel stops recognizing it: from then on every visitor becomes a single address, and the login attempt limit applies to everyone together — five wrong attempts by anyone would lock you out too. It fails by becoming stricter, which is the quietest way to break.

fw.port25Advice.html: Advice: leave it off. The bots knocking on port 25 usually try to use you as an open relay, but Postfix already turns them away with Relay access denied: that noise in the logs is harmless. Turning it on gains almost nothing in security and risks losing legitimate incoming mail.

fw.port25What.html: What it does: normally the country whitelist only protects the login ports (587, 465, 143, 993, 110, 995), where attackers try to guess passwords. Port 25 stays open to everyone instead: it is the port other mail servers (Gmail, Microsoft, your friends' and customers' servers) use to deliver your incoming mail.
fw.port25When.html: When to turn it on: only if you are 100% sure nobody will ever write to you from a mail server in a country outside the whitelist (for example China, India, Vietnam, Brazil). Even a small foreign supplier could send you legitimate invoices or notices.

jc.findTimeHint.html: The period in which attempts are counted. Recommended: 1 h (covers slow attacks too).

jc.pfDdosCatches: Huge numbers of connections from the same IP in a few seconds.
jc.pfDdosMisses: Attacks spread over many different IPs.
jc.pfMoreCatches: SASL failures + improper command pipelining + basic rejects.
jc.pfMoreMisses: Probes that only connect/disconnect with auth=0/N.
jc.pfSaslCatches: Only "SASL authentication failed" (real login attempts with a wrong password).
jc.pfSaslMisses: SMTP scanners and bots that try AUTH and disconnect without an explicit SASL error.

lg.brutePanelDesc.html: Panel brute force: failed logins to the admin panel (jail mail-panel-auth).
lg.bruteSmtpCatch: Finds: failed SMTP logins (Postfix SASL), the real attempts to break into outgoing mail.
lg.bruteSmtpDesc.html: SMTP brute force (SASL): failed SMTP logins on Postfix. They are real attacks on outgoing mail: if you see many from the same IP, Fail2ban should ban it (jail postfix-auth).
lg.connectionsCatch: Finds: every incoming connection (to see who contacts you).
lg.connectionsDesc.html: Connections: every TCP connection opened and closed towards the mail server. Useful to see who contacts you in real time.
lg.errorsCatch: Finds: ALL errors and warnings of ANY service. A good start when something is wrong.
lg.errorsDesc.html: Errors and warnings of every service: the first filter to try when something is wrong and you do not know where to look.
lg.knownScannersCatch: Finds: the names of scanners known to be harmless. Useful to recognize the noise.
lg.knownScannersDesc.html: Known bots and scanners: only the hosts whose name identifies them as public security scanners. Harmless: recognize them so you do not mistake them for attacks.
lg.mailBounceCatch: Finds: rejected, bounced or deferred messages. The place to look when someone says mail does not arrive.
lg.mailBounceDesc.html: Bounced and rejected: messages NOT delivered (permanent bounces, deferred, rejected). The first place to look when someone says their mail did not arrive.
lg.mailSentDesc.html: Mail delivered: the delivered messages. If you look for a specific one, add the sender or the recipient to the filter.

lg.scannersCatch: Finds: internet scanners (Censys, Shodan, BinaryEdge and similar) probing the mail ports with malformed requests. They are NOT attacks, just internet noise.
lg.scannersDesc.html: Internet scanners: probes from public scanners (Censys, Shodan, BinaryEdge...) knocking on the mail ports with malformed requests. They are NOT attacks, just internet noise: Postfix answers that it speaks TLS and that is the end of it.
lg.spamDesc.html: Spam and viruses: anti-spam (Rspamd) and antivirus (ClamAV) events: messages marked as spam, scores, viruses found.

pa.after.html: After downloading: on a Mac open the file, then confirm it in System Settings → General → VPN & Device Management. On iPhone or iPad «Profile Downloaded» shows at the top of Settings. The profile is not signed, so it is marked as unverified: that is normal for a profile you generated yourself. If this device has a profile downloaded before 30 October 2026, remove it before installing this one: it has a different identifier, and the two would stay side by side with the same mailbox twice.
pa.intro1.html: Apple Mail does not use the SRV records nor the XML file Thunderbird looks for: it relies on an internal list of known providers, and for your own server no Apple document describes automatic discovery. The way Apple documents is another one: the configuration profile.
pa.intro2.html: You download the file, open it, and the mailbox is created with server, ports and encryption already right. The password is not in the file — it would end up in the Downloads folder in plain text: Mail asks for it once, the same for incoming and outgoing.
pa.sets.html: The profile sets IMAP on {imap} and SMTP on {smtp}, both with direct TLS, with the full address as user name. Port 465 is chosen on purpose: the Apple schema has a single «use SSL» switch and does not tell STARTTLS apart, while on that port Postfix speaks TLS from the first byte — no ambiguity.

server.adns.fixRefused: On {name} the record is not right ({what}) and Cloudflare refused the fix: {e}

server.adns.manyDmarcEdit: On {name} there are {n} DMARC records. With two records both are discarded (RFC 9989) and I would not even know which one to change: only one must be left first.
server.adns.multiDmarc: There are {n} DMARC records on the same name: RFC 9989 discards them ALL. The policy is not "the first of the two": there is none.
server.adns.multiSpf: There are {n} SPF records on the same name: RFC 7208 §4.5 says the result is "permerror", that is SPF does not work at all. They must be merged into one.
server.adns.needDest: The mailbox to deliver the reports to is needed.
server.adns.noAccount: No Cloudflare account assigned to {d}: without one, the panel cannot write records. Assign one in the Cloudflare accounts tab.
server.adns.noDmarcToEdit: On {name} there is no DMARC record to change: it must be created first.
server.adns.noHostname: The mail server's hostname is not configured: without it, the record would point to nothing. Set it first in the panel settings.
server.adns.noIpSpf: The panel cannot work out the server's public IP, and an SPF without an address ("v=spf1 ip4: mx -all") is syntactically invalid: it would be discarded as a whole. The IP must be resolved first on the DNS page.
server.adns.noIpWrite: I cannot work out the server's public IP. Writing "v=spf1 ip4: mx -all" would produce an invalid record, which recipients discard as a whole: better no SPF than a broken one. Resolve the IP first on the DNS page.
server.adns.noRotation: SPF and DMARC contain no keys: they are public policy declarations. They change when the server or the policy changes, not on a schedule. That is why the panel offers no rotation: it would be fake maintenance, and every automatic SPF change is a chance to stop the mail.
server.adns.noneNow: You are back to observation only: no mail is blocked.
server.adns.notChanged: Cloudflare accepted the change, but reading the zone again the record does not appear changed. Look at it in Cloudflare before trying again.
server.adns.notMailAddr: "{d}" does not have the form of an email address.
server.adns.onlyP: Only the value of "p" changes. All the rest of the record stays as it is.
server.adns.opt.autoconfigNeeds: The record alone is not enough: for it to be useful, the configuration file (/mail/config-v1.1.xml) must answer on that name. The panel serves it: the "Automatic client configuration" tab below really downloads it and says whether it arrives. Do not count on the two SRV records for Thunderbird: it does not read them (it is written in the same tab).
server.adns.opt.autoconfigWhat: The address where Thunderbird goes to look for ready-made settings.
server.adns.opt.imapsWhat: It tells clients where to get incoming mail (IMAP over TLS, port 993). It works on its own: the client queries the DNS and works out host and port without anything else (RFC 6186 §4).
server.adns.opt.stsNeeds: On its own it does nothing: the panel must also serve the policy on that name (it is configured from below) and the certificate must cover mta-sts.<domain>. The TXT record that declares the policy is created AFTER, and only when the policy really answers.
server.adns.opt.stsWhat: The address where sending servers go to read the MTA-STS policy.
server.adns.opt.submissionWhat: It tells clients where to hand over outgoing mail (submission, port 587). It works on its own, like the one above.
server.adns.othersRemoved: The other MTA-STS records were removed: {list}
server.adns.policyActive: The policy is "p={p}". Remember that this policy acts on mail right away.
server.adns.policyNone: The policy is "p={p}": it blocks nothing, it serves to receive the reports and see who sends on your behalf before deciding. It is tightened later, once the reports have been read.
server.adns.policySame: The policy was already "p={p}": I did not touch anything.
server.adns.propagation: Propagation usually takes a few minutes.
server.adns.proxied: The record is proxied by Cloudflare (orange cloud): that way it no longer answers with the host but with Cloudflare's addresses, and the mail client does not find the server. It must be set to "DNS only".
server.adns.quarantineNow: From now on mail that does not authenticate ends up in spam. It is the intermediate step: if no surprises appear in the reports, you then move to reject.
server.adns.readBoxes: I cannot read mailboxes and aliases: {m}
server.adns.recordConflict: On {name} there is already a {existingKind} record ({content}). A {kind} cannot sit on the same name together with other data: which of the two must stay has to be decided first.
server.adns.rejectNow: From now on mail that does not authenticate on behalf of this domain is rejected: if some service of yours was not authorized, it stops being delivered. Look at the reports in the next days.
server.adns.ruaInside: Since the reports address stays inside the domain itself, no authorization record is needed (RFC 9990 §4): it just has to be deliverable somewhere.
server.adns.ruaMissing: The record would say to send the reports to {a}, which however does not exist: neither a mailbox nor an alias. RFC 9989 §5.1.4 has the mailbox created first and then the record, for a practical reason: once the DMARC is published, the reports start arriving right away and they would all bounce. Create the alias below first, then come back to create the DMARC.
server.adns.ruaOutside: The rua points outside the domain: without the record {r} (RFC 9990 §4) the reports are not sent.
server.adns.spfNotAuth: The existing SPF does not authorize this server: it contains neither the IP {ip} nor an "mx" or "a" mechanism.
server.adns.spfOthers: An existing SPF can authorize other services to send for this domain (newsletters, business software): replacing it would make them stop working, and you would notice days later. Look at it in Cloudflare and, if needed, add "ip4:{ip}" to what is already there.
server.adns.stsCleaned: On {name} there were {n} MTA-STS records, and with more than one senders act as if MTA-STS were not there (RFC 8461 §3.1). Now there is only one, with the right id. Removed: {list}.
server.adns.stsManyDelFail: On {name} there are {n} MTA-STS records, and with more than one senders act as if MTA-STS were not there (RFC 8461 §3.1). Cloudflare refused to remove "{c}": {e}
server.adns.stsPublished: MTA-STS record published on {name}. The policy is already reachable, so the declaration is kept right from the start.
server.adns.stsReadMany: Cloudflare accepted the changes, but reading the zone again there are {n} MTA-STS records on {name}: {list}.
server.adns.stsReadNone: Cloudflare accepted the changes, but reading the zone again there is no MTA-STS record on {name}.

server.autoconf.noServerName: I cannot find the server_name line in the file: I do not edit blindly.
server.autoconf.noneTried: I could not try any domain, so I do not know whether the file arrives. "I did not check" is not "it does not work", but it is not "fine" either.
server.autoconf.notArriving: The file does not arrive for {n} domains out of {tot}: {list}
server.autoconf.notConfigFile: It answers 200 but what comes back is not the configuration file: probably it is the webmail or an error page.
server.autoconf.otherDomain: The file comes back, but it does not declare the domain {d}: it is the file of another domain.
server.autoconf.publicSurface: I do not touch nginx.conf. The public surface on 443 is already installed (conf.d/{file}) and it is what answers for autoconfig.<domain> and mta-sts.<domain>, serving both this file and the MTA-STS policy. Adding those names to the webmail server_name would take them away from it, together with the rate limits, the GET/HEAD restriction, the 404 on everything else and the log watched by the fail2ban jail. If the file does not arrive, the cause is elsewhere: almost always it is the panel web server, which is what generates the XML — a 502 says exactly that.
server.autoconf.reloadFailed: The configuration was valid but the reload failed: I put back the previous one. The system said: {out}
server.autoconf.routeElsewhere: The route is not in {conf} but in another configuration file — the one of the "Port 443" tab — and that is perfectly fine: what matters is that the file arrives.
server.autoconf.serverNameNoSemicolon: The server_name line does not end with ';': unexpected file, I do not touch it.
server.autoconf.status: The server answers {c} instead of 200: the file is not served at that name.
server.autoconf.stillNotArriving: I wrote and reloaded, but the file still does not arrive: {why} I put back the previous configuration, because a change that does not achieve what it was made for is just one more change to remember. Copy in {copy}.
server.autoconf.stsLost: I put back the previous configuration and reloaded: the change had made the MTA-STS policy of {list} stop answering. Those domains have the TXT record published, so a policy that does not answer is a broken promise: better no autoconfig than this.

server.dnsg.ruaAuthOk: Authorization for out-of-domain reports present on {name}.
server.dnsg.ruaCheck: TO CHECK: the reports address is on another domain and I cannot find the authorization. If the two domains belong to different organizations, a TXT must be published on {name} with the value "v=DMARC1" (RFC 9990 §4), otherwise the reports are not even sent. If instead they are two names of the same organization, nothing is needed.
server.dnsg.spfInclude.one: Cannot be determined from here: the authorization depends on 1 term that refers to other records. The server is not listed directly.
server.dnsg.spfInclude.other: Cannot be determined from here: the authorization depends on {n} terms that refer to other records. The server is not listed directly.
server.dnsg.spfNotAuth: The SPF does not authorize this server: it contains neither the IP {ip} nor an "mx" or "a" mechanism.
server.dnsg.spfOkA: OK through the "a" mechanism: it holds as long as the A record points here.
server.dnsg.spfOkMx: OK through the "mx" mechanism: it holds as long as the MX points here (see the MX check above).
server.dnsg.srvBoth: It points to {dest} on port {port}, instead of {h} on {wait}.
server.dnsg.srvHost: The port is right, but it points to {dest} instead of {h}.
server.dnsg.srvPort: The host is right, but the port is {port} instead of {wait}: clients would try to connect where nobody answers.
server.dnsg.stsActive: Active: the record is there and the policy answers.
server.dnsg.stsMany: There are {n} v=STSv1 records on _mta-sts.{d}: for senders it is like having none (RFC 8461 §3.1), so MTA-STS is not active. Only one must remain: when the policy answers, the "Activate MTA-STS" sequence keeps the one with the right id and removes the others.
server.dnsg.stsNotServed: THE RECORD IS THERE BUT THE POLICY DOES NOT ANSWER. You are publicly declaring that you have MTA-STS, and whoever goes to read it on https://mta-sts.{d}/.well-known/mta-sts.txt finds nothing: {e} Senders go on as if you did not have it (RFC 8461 §3.3), so it does not break mail — but it is a declaration you do not keep. Either it is served, or the record is removed.
server.dnsg.stsOff: Not active. It is not an oversight: MTA-STS requires the policy to be reachable from the whole world on https://mta-sts.{d} (port 443), because sending servers read it. On a server closed to external IPs it cannot work, and publishing only the record would declare a protection that is absent.
server.dnsg.stsUnknown: Cannot tell whether the record is there: {why}.
server.dnsrules.dmarcBadP: The "p" tag is "{p}", which is not an expected value: the values are none, quarantine or reject.
server.dnsrules.dmarcMany: There are {n} DMARC records on the same name. RFC 9989 says that in this case ALL of them are discarded: the policy is not "the first of the two", there is none at all. Leave only one record.
server.dnsrules.dmarcNoP: The "p" tag is missing. RFC 9989 treats it as "none", that is, no action: better to write it, so it is clear what is being asked.
server.dnsrules.dmarcNoRua: The "rua" tag is missing: without it, no report arrives and there is no way to know who sends on behalf of this domain. RFC 9989 §5.1.4 starts right here, before even choosing a policy.
server.dnsrules.dmarcNone: No valid DMARC record. Without it, anyone can write this domain in the From: field and nobody has instructions on what to do with it.
server.dnsrules.dmarcPct: Whoever wanted to apply the policy gradually now uses "t=y", which applies it one level milder.
server.dnsrules.dmarcRemovedTag: The record contains "{tag}", which RFC 9989 removed: today it does nothing.
server.dnsrules.dmarcTest: There is "t=y": the declared policy is applied one level milder (reject becomes quarantine, quarantine becomes none). It is the test mode, to be removed when the policy should really apply.
server.dnsrules.dmarcUnknownTag: Tag "{tag}" is not defined by RFC 9989. The specification says to ignore unknown tags, so it breaks nothing, but it does nothing either.
server.dnsrules.ruaNoDomain: The address "{addr}" in rua has no domain.
server.dnsrules.spfDirect.one: Direct DNS lookups: {n} of 10. The real count is higher, because one term leads into other lookups that can only be counted by resolving them.
server.dnsrules.spfDirect.other: Direct DNS lookups: {n} of 10. The real count is higher, because {includes} terms lead into other lookups that can only be counted by resolving them.
server.dnsrules.spfLookups: The record already makes {n} DNS lookups on its own: the RFC 7208 §4.6.4 limit is 10, beyond which the result is "permerror".
server.dnsrules.spfMany: There are {n} SPF records on the same name. RFC 7208 §4.5 says that in this case the result is "permerror": SPF does not half fail, it stops working entirely. Leave ONE record only, merging by hand what is needed from both.

server.dnsrules.spfPlusAll: The record ends with "+all": it authorizes anyone to send for this domain. It is like having no SPF, but looking as if you had it.

Updating it while it is running, the JVM in memory no longer matches the files on disk and the panel can NO longer start processes: from then on every command it launches fails silently, including locking the packages again, and every status it reports becomes false. Do NOT update it from here: use the "Panel JVM update" tab, which does it with a detached script — it packs the current Java as a way back, stops the panel, updates, checks that java answers and starts the panel again on its own.
server.um.changeLocks.16: It affects the TLS of Postfix, Dovecot and nginx together. A major change can stop accepting old protocols or ciphers: old clients might no longer connect.
server.um.changeLocks.2: CERTAIN BREAKAGE. Dovecot 2.4 does not accept 2.3 configurations: it does not start at all, it does not just log warnings. Two new mandatory directives are needed (dovecot_config_version and dovecot_storage_version), passdb and userdb must have a name, mail_location has been split into several mail_* settings, and the single-letter variables (%u %d %n %h) have been removed. THIS PANEL generates exactly that syntax: after the update mail stops, and regenerating the configuration from the panel would not bring it back. The configuration generator must be adapted first, then the package.
server.um.changeLocks.3: Do NOT update it from here: use the "Roundcube update" tab, which also updates the schema. A major Roundcube version change requires updating the database schema (bin/updatedb.sh): until you run it the webmail stays unusable. The package is also tied to the PHP version (roundcube-phpNN): changing PHP means changing this too.
server.um.changeLocks.4: This panel's scripts name a precise PHP version in paths, in the php-fpm socket and in the nginx configuration of the webmail. Updating the package without first adapting the panel leaves the webmail without PHP. roundcube-phpNN must also be kept aligned.
server.um.changeLocks.5: On FreeBSD the major MySQL versions are DIFFERENT, conflicting packages: no pkg upgrade takes you from 8.0 to 8.4. And at its first start the new version rewrites the data dictionary, which cannot be undone. It must be done as a migration of its own, with a cold copy taken while the database is stopped.
server.um.changeLocks.6: It must be kept aligned with the MySQL server: updating it alone puts the protocol versions out of step.
server.um.changeLocks.7: Postfix updates are usually painless, but the compatibility level (compatibility_level) changes the defaults between major versions: after the update check the startup logs. Also watch the package flavor: without MySQL support, Postfix no longer reads the virtual mailboxes and rejects mail.
server.um.changeLocks.8: Major versions change some configuration options and the format of some keys in Redis. After the update check that outgoing DKIM signing still works.
server.um.changeLocks.9: It is rspamd's memory: Bayesian statistics, greylisting and limits. The update is usually compatible, but if the dump file were not read back, rspamd would restart without training.

sts.intro1.html: Between two mail servers TLS is opportunistic: if the recipient does not offer STARTTLS, the message leaves anyway, in clear text. An attacker in the middle can strip that offer as it passes, and the sender has no way to notice. MTA-STS closes that door: it declares in advance that your servers always have TLS, and that whoever cannot manage it must not deliver.
sts.intro2.html: It takes three pieces together, which is why the record is not created by itself: an mta-sts CNAME, the policy served over HTTPS on that name with a certificate valid for that name, and only at the end the TXT record that declares it. The TXT is not published until the policy really answers: it would be a public promise you do not keep.

up.release: Moving to a new FreeBSD release
up.releaseIntro.html:
What the panel does. The preliminary checks, the copy of /etc, the way back (a ZFS boot environment you return to with one command), the pending patches, then freebsd-update install repeated as many times as needed — reading what freebsd-update asks for and acting on it — the reboots, and the final check against the inventory taken before. It remembers where it is, so it survives the reboots.
What is left to you, and only that: the first command, freebsd-update -r <version> upgrade. Not for the confirmation it asks — that would be trivial — but because it may open an editor to merge the files in /etc: they include master.passwd, rc.conf and the Postfix files, and a merge decided by automation is the way to break something without anyone noticing. It rarely happens, but when it does it takes a person.

up.w443Intro1.html: Two features need port 443 because the protocols allow no other port: the MTA-STS policy, read by sending servers all over the world, and the Thunderbird configuration file. Opening that port exposes something, so that something must be as little as possible.
up.w443Intro2.html: The block the panel installs is separate from the webmail one on 8443 — if it were added inside it, it would inherit Roundcube's root and the PHP handler, opening a whole application to serve two text files. It has default_server, so no other site can answer on that port; only two exact location blocks and 404 for everything else; only GET and HEAD; rate and connection limits per address; short timeouts. The MTA-STS policy is a static file: a request there never reaches the panel or the database.
up.webIntro1.html: The panel contains two install scripts that write different nginx configurations: one puts a block on port 80 that serves the webmail in clear text, the other only the encrypted 443. Looking at the code you cannot tell which one built this machine.
up.webIntro2.html: This diagnosis reads nginx -T, the full configuration as nginx really sees it, plus the listening ports, the pf rules and the fail2ban jails. It changes nothing. And if a command fails it says so, instead of concluding that all is well.

up.svcUsersIntro1.html: Every service has its own user, and root only where it is needed by design: the main processes that open the ports and then drop privileges, fail2ban that drives pf, the panel. This check reads the running processes, the php-fpm pools and root's crontab, and warns if a service runs as root without needing it or shares its user with another one. It changes nothing.

su.caption: The mail services and the users of their processes
server.su.rootWhy.postfix: Root only for the master process: it opens the mail ports (25, 465, 587) and delivers system mail. What talks to the Internet (smtpd) runs as postfix.
server.su.rootWhy.dovecot: Root only for the main process, the configuration and the log: it opens the IMAP and POP3 ports and starts logins as dovenull and mailboxes as vmail. Passwords are looked up as dovecot.
server.su.rootWhy.nginx: Root only for the master process: it opens the web ports and reads the TLS keys, which only root can read. Requests are served by the worker processes as www.
server.su.rootWhy.phpFpm: Root only for the master process, which runs no pages: it creates the webmail's socket owned by roundcube with group www, so only nginx and Roundcube can use it. Pages run in the pool as roundcube.
server.su.rootWhy.fail2ban: Root because it controls the pf firewall (/dev/pf is root only) and reads the mail logs, which only root can read.
server.su.rootWhy.mailPanel: Root only for the part that manages the machine (packages, services, firewall, configurations, boot environments), which opens no ports. The web part, the one that answers on the network, runs as the mailpanel user and hands it the requests on a local socket.
